*Translator's note:* See note at {{Isaiah 13:1|Isa 13:1}}.

*Study note:* The phrase is quite cryptic, at least to the modern reader. Verse {{Isaiah 21:9|9}} seems to indicate that this message pertains to Babylon. Southern Mesopotamia was known as the Sealand in ancient times because of its proximity to the Persian Gulf. Perhaps the reference to Babylon as a “wilderness” foreshadows the destruction that would overtake the city, making it like an uninhabited wilderness.

*Translator's note:* Or “in the Negev” (NASB).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a severe revelation has been related to me.”

*Study note:* This is often interpreted to mean “all the groaning” that Babylon has caused others.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “my waist is filled with shaking [or “anguish”].”

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps, “bent over [in pain]”; cf. NRSV “I am bowed down.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “wanders”; perhaps here, “is confused.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “shuddering terrifies me.”

*Translator's note:* The precise meaning of the verb in this line is debated. Some prefer to derive the form from the homonymic צָפֹה (tsafoh, “keep watch”) and translate “post a guard” (cf. KJV “watch in the watchtower”; ASV “set the watch”).

*Translator's note:* The verbal forms in the first three lines are infinitives absolute, which are functioning here as finite verbs. It is uncertain if the forms should have an imperatival or indicative/descriptive force here.

*Study note:* Smearing the shields with oil would make them more flexible and effective in battle. See J. N. Oswalt, *Isaiah* (NICOT), 1:394.
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term translated “Lord” here and in vv. {{Isaiah 21:8|8}}, {{Isaiah 21:16|16}} is אֲדֹנָי (ʾadonay).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has, “the lion,” but this makes little sense here. אַרְיֵה (ʾaryeh, “lion”) probably needs to be emended to an original הָרֹאֶה (haroʾeh, “the one who sees”), i.e., the guard mentioned previously in v. {{Isaiah 21:6|6}}. The Dead Sea Scrolls (1Q Isaa) and the Syriac support an original הָרֹאֶה (haroʾeh, “the one who sees”).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term translated “Lord” here is אֲדֹנָי (ʾadonay). Some translations take this to refer to the Lord (cf. NAB, NASB, NRSV), while others take it to refer to the guard’s human master (“my lord”; cf. NIV, NLT).

*Translator's note:* Or “[with] teams of horses,” or perhaps, “with a pair of horsemen.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he answered and said” (so KJV, ASV).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “My trampled one, and the son of the threshing floor.”

*Translator's note:* The noun דּוּמָה (dumah) means “silence,” but here it is a proper name, probably referring to a site in northern Arabia or to the nation of Edom. See BDB 189 s.v. II דּוּמָה. If Dumah was an area in northern Arabia, it would be of interest to the Edomites because of its strategic position on trade routes which they used. See J. N. Oswalt, *Isaiah* (NICOT), 1:398.

*Study note:* Seir is another name for Edom. See BDB 973 s.v. שֵׂעִיר.

*Study note:* The “night” probably here symbolizes distress and difficult times. See BDB 539 s.v. לַיְלָה.

*Study note:* Dumah will experience some relief, but it will be short-lived as *night* returns.

*Study note:* The point of the watchman’s final instructions (“if you want to ask, ask; come again”) is unclear. Perhaps they are included to add realism to the dramatic portrayal. The watchman sends the questioner away with the words, “Feel free to come back and ask again.”

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term translated “Lord” here is אֲדֹנָי (ʾadonay).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in still a year, like the years of a hired worker.” See the note at {{Isaiah 16:14|16:14}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the remnant of the number of the bow, the mighty men of the sons of Kedar, will be few.”

*Translator's note:* Or “for” (KJV, ASV, NAB, NASB, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* See note at {{Isaiah 13:1|Isa 13:1}}.

*Study note:* The following message pertains to Jerusalem. The significance of referring to the city as *the Valley of Vision* is uncertain. Perhaps the Hinnom Valley is in view, but why it is associated with a prophetic revelatory “vision” is not entirely clear. Maybe the Hinnom Valley is called this because the destruction that will take place there is the focal point of this prophetic message (see v. {{Isaiah 21:5|5}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “What to you, then?”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the boisterous town.” The phrase is parallel to “the noisy city” in the preceding line.

*Study note:* Apparently they died from starvation during the siege that preceded the final conquest of the city. See J. N. Oswalt, *Isaiah* (NICOT), 1:409.

*Translator's note:* Verse {{Isaiah 22:3|3}} reads literally, “All your leaders ran away; apart from a bow they were captured; all your found ones were captured together; to a distant place they fled.” J. N. Oswalt (*Isaiah* [NICOT], 1:403, n. 3) suggests that the lines of the verse are arranged chiastically; lines 1 and 4 go together, while lines 2 and 3 are parallel. To translate the lines in the order they appear in the Hebrew text is misleading to the English reader, who is likely unfamiliar with, or at least insensitive to, chiastic parallelism. Consequently, the main translation arranges the lines as follows: line 1 (Hebrew) = line 1 (in translation); line 2 (Hebrew) = line 4 (in translation); line 3 (Hebrew) = line 3 (in translation); line 4 (Hebrew) = line 2 (in translation).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all your found ones.” To achieve tighter parallelism (see “your leaders”) some prefer to emend the form to אַמִּיצַיִךְ (ʾammitsayikh, “your strong ones”) or to נֶאֱמָצַיִךְ (neʾematsayikh, “your strengthened ones”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “apart from [i.e., without] a bow they were captured”; cf. NAB, NRSV “without the use of a bow.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “look away from me” (so KJV, ASV, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “don’t hurry” (so NCV).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the daughter of my people.” “Daughter” is here used metaphorically to express the speaker’s emotional attachment to his people, as well as their vulnerability and weakness.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew term translated “Sovereign” here and in vv. {{Isaiah 22:12|12}}, {{Isaiah 22:14|14}}, {{Isaiah 22:15|15}} is אֲדֹנָי (ʾadonay).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “For [there is] a day of panic, and trampling, and confusion for the master, the Lord of Heaven’s Armies [traditionally, “the Lord of hosts”].”

*Translator's note:* The traditional accentuation of the Hebrew text suggests that this phrase goes with what precedes.

*Translator's note:* The precise meaning of this statement is unclear. Some take קִר (qir) as “wall” and interpret the verb to mean “tear down.” However, tighter parallelism (note the reference to crying for help in the next line) is achieved if one takes both the verb and noun from a root, attested in Ugaritic and Arabic, meaning “make a sound.” See J. N. Oswalt, *Isaiah* (NICOT), 1:404, n. 5.

*Study note:* Perhaps “the hill” refers to the temple mount.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[with] the chariots of men, horsemen.”

*Study note:* A distant region in the direction of Mesopotamia; see {{Amos 1:5|Amos 1:5}}; {{Amos 9:7|9:7}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Kir uncovers” (so NAB, NIV).

*Study note:* The Elamites and men of Kir may here symbolize a fierce army from a distant land. If this oracle anticipates a Babylonian conquest of the city (see {{Isaiah 39:5|39:5-7}}), then the Elamites and men of Kir are perhaps viewed here as mercenaries in the Babylonian army. See J. N. Oswalt, *Isaiah* (NICOT), 1:410.

*Translator's note:* The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in {{Isaiah 2:2|2:2}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “taking a stand, take their stand.” The infinitive absolute emphasizes the following finite verb. The translation attempts to bring out this emphasis with the adverb “confidently.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he,” i.e., the enemy invader. NASB, by its capitalization of the pronoun, takes this to refer to the Lord.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “covering.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in that day” (so KJV); likewise at the beginning of v. {{Isaiah 22:12|12}}.

*Study note:* Perhaps this refers to a royal armory, or to Solomon’s “House of the Forest of Lebanon,” where weapons may have been kept (see {{1 Kings 10:16|1 Kgs 10:16-17}}).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the breaks of the City of David, you saw that they were many.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “you demolished the houses to fortify the wall.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “look at”; NAB, NRSV “did not look to.”

*Translator's note:* The antecedent of the third feminine singular suffix here and in the next line is unclear. The closest feminine noun is “pool” in the first half of the verse. Perhaps this “old pool” symbolizes the entire city, which had prospered because of God’s provision and protection through the years.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “did not see.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for baldness and the wearing of sackcloth.” See the note at {{Isaiah 15:2|15:2}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “happiness and joy.”

*Translator's note:* The prophet here quotes what the fatalistic people are saying. The introductory “you say” is supplied in the translation for clarification; the concluding verb “we die” makes it clear the people are speaking. The six verbs translated as imperatives are actually infinitives absolute, functioning here as finite verbs.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “it was revealed in my ears [by?] the Lord of Heaven’s Armies [traditionally, “the Lord of hosts”].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Certainly this sin will not be atoned for until you die.” This does not imply that their death will bring atonement; rather it emphasizes that their sin is unpardonable. The statement has the form of an oath.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who is over the house” (so ASV); NASB “who is in charge of the royal household.”

*Translator's note:* The words “and tell him” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “What to you here? And who to you here?” The point of the second question is not entirely clear. The interpretation reflected in the translation is based on the following context, which suggests that Shebna has no right to think of himself so highly and arrange such an extravagant burial place for himself.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “that you chisel out.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “will throw you with a throwing.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “O man” (so NASB); NAB “mortal man”; NRSV “my fellow.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and the one who wraps you [will] wrap.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he will tightly [or “surely”] wind you [with] winding like a ball, to a land broad of hands [i.e., “sides”].”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and there the chariots of your splendor.”

*Study note:* Apparently the reference to chariots alludes to Shebna’s excessive pride, which in turn brings disgrace to the royal family.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “I will push you away from.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “he will throw you down.” The shift from the first to third person is peculiar and abrupt, but certainly not unprecedented in Hebrew poetry. See GKC 462 §144.*p*. The third person may be indefinite (“one will throw you down”), in which case the passive translation is justified.
*Translator's note:* Or “in that day.” The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in {{Isaiah 2:2|2:2}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and your dominion I will place in his hand.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “a father to.” The Hebrew term אָב (ʾav, “father”) is here used metaphorically of one who protects and supports those under his care and authority, like a father does his family. For another example of this metaphorical use of the word, see {{Job 29:16|Job 29:16}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “house.”

*Study note:* This may refer to a literal insignia worn by the chief administrator. Even so, it would still symbolize the administrator’s authority to grant or exclude access to the king. See J. N. Oswalt, *Isaiah* (NICOT), 1:422.

*Study note:* The metaphor depicts how secure his position will be.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and he will become a glorious throne for the house of his father.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and all the glory of the house of his father they will hang on him.” The Lord returns to the peg metaphor of v. {{Isaiah 22:23|23a}}. Eliakim’s secure position of honor will bring benefits and jobs to many others in the family.

*Translator's note:* The precise meaning and derivation of this word are uncertain. Cf. KJV, ASV, NRSV “the issue”; CEV “relatives.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “all the small vessels, from the vessels that are bowls to all the vessels that are jars.” The picture is that of a single peg holding the weight of all kinds of containers hung from it.

*Translator's note:* Or “In that day” (KJV).

*Study note:* Eliakim’s authority, though seemingly secure, will eventually be removed, and with it his family’s prominence.

*Translator's note:* Or “for” (KJV, NAB, NASB, NRSV).

*Translator's note:* See note at {{Isaiah 13:1|Isa 13:1}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “ships of Tarshish.” This probably refers to large ships either made in or capable of traveling to the distant, western port of Tarshish.

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text reads literally, “for it is destroyed, from a house, from entering.” The translation assumes that the mem (מ) on בַּיִת (bayit) was originally an enclitic mem suffixed to the preceding verb. This assumption allows one to take בַּיִת as the subject of the preceding verb. It is used in a metaphorical sense for the port city of Tyre. The preposition min (מִן) prefixed to בּוֹא (boʾ) indicates negative consequence: “so that no one can enter.” See BDB 583 s.v. מִן 7.b.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Kittim,” a designation for the people of Cyprus. See *HALOT* 504-05 s.v. כִּתִּיִּים.

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text ({{Isaiah 23:2|23:2b-3a}}) reads literally, “merchant of Sidon, the one who crosses the sea, they filled you, and on the deep waters.” Instead of מִלְאוּךְ (milʾukh, “they filled you”) the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa reads מלאכיך (“your messengers”). The translation assumes an emendation of מִלְאוּךְ to מַלְאָכָו (malʾakhav, “his messengers”), taking the vav (ו) on וּבְמַיִם (uvemayim) as improperly placed; instead it should be the final letter of the preceding word.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “seed of Shihor.” “Shihor” probably refers to the east branch of the Nile. See Jer 2:18 and BDB 1009 s.v. שִׁיחוֹר.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the harvest of the Nile.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[is] her revenue.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “merchandise”; KJV, ASV “a mart of nations”; NLT “the merchandise mart of the world.”

*Translator's note:* J. N. Oswalt (*Isaiah* [NICOT], 1:430-31) sees here a reference to Yam, the Canaanite god of the sea. He interprets the phrase מָעוֹז הַיָּם (maʿoz hayyam, “fortress of the sea”) as a title of Yam, translating “Mighty One of the Sea.” A more traditional view is that the phrase refers to Sidon.

*Translator's note:* Or “virgins” (KJV, ASV, NAB, NASB).

*Study note:* The sea is personified here as a lamenting childless woman. The foreboding language anticipates the following announcement of Tyre’s demise, viewed here as a child of the sea, as it were.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “they will be in pain at the report of Tyre.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “Is this to you, boisterous one?” The pronoun “you” is masculine plural, like the imperatives in v. {{Isaiah 23:6|6}}, so it is likely addressed to the Egyptians and residents of the coast. “Boisterous one” is a feminine singular form, probably referring to the personified city of Tyre.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “in the days of antiquity [is] her beginning.”

*Translator's note:* The precise meaning of הַמַּעֲטִירָה (hammaʿatirah) is uncertain. The form is a Hiphil participle from עָטַר (ʿatar), a denominative verb derived from עֲטָרָה (ʿatarah, “crown, wreath”). The participle may mean “one who wears a crown” or “one who distributes crowns.” In either case, Tyre’s prominence in the international political arena is in view.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the honored” (so NASB, NRSV); NIV “renowned.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the pride of all the beauty.”

*Text-critical note:* This meaning of this verse is unclear. The Hebrew text reads literally, “Cross over your land, like the Nile, daughter of Tarshish, there is no more waistband.” The translation assumes an emendation of מֵזַח (mezakh, “waistband”) to מָחֹז (makhoz, “harbor, marketplace”; see {{Psalm 107:30|Ps 107:30}}). The term עָבַר (ʿavar, “cross over”) is probably used here of traveling over the water (as in v. {{Isaiah 23:6|6}}). The command is addressed to personified Tarshish, who here represents her merchants. The Qumran scroll 1QIsaa has עבדי (“work, cultivate”) instead of עִבְרִי (ʿivri, “cross over”). In this case one might translate “Cultivate your land, like they do the Nile region” (cf. NIV, CEV). The point would be that the people of Tarshish should turn to agriculture because they will no longer be able to get what they need through the marketplace in Tyre.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his hand he stretched out over the sea.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the Lord.” For stylistic reasons the pronoun (“he”) has been used in the translation here.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “concerning Canaan, to destroy her fortresses.” NIV, NLT translate “Canaan” as “Phoenicia” here.

*Translator's note:* Or “violated, raped,” the point being that Daughter Sidon has lost her virginity in the most brutal manner possible.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[to the] Kittim, get up, cross over; even there there will be no rest for you.” On “Kittim” see the note on “Cyprus” at v. {{Isaiah 23:1|1}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “this people [that] is not.”

*Translator's note:* For the meaning of this word, see *HALOT* 118 s.v. *בַּחוּן.

*Translator's note:* Or “laid bare.” For the meaning of this word, see *HALOT* 889 s.v. ערר.

*Study note:* This verse probably refers to the Assyrian destruction of Babylon.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “ships of Tarshish.” See the note at v. {{Isaiah 23:1|1}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “in that day” (KJV). The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in {{Isaiah 2:2|2:2}}.

*Study note:* The number *70* is probably used in a stereotypical, nonliteral sense here to indicate a long period of time that satisfies completely the demands of God’s judgment.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like the days of a king.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “At the end of 70 years it will be for Tyre like the song of the prostitute.”

*Translator's note:* The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in {{Isaiah 2:2|2:2}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “visit [with favor]” (cf. KJV, NAB, NASB, NRSV); NIV “will deal with.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and she will return to her [prostitute’s] wages and engage in prostitution with all the kingdoms of the earth on the face of the earth.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for eating to fullness and for beautiful covering[s].”

*Study note:* The point of this verse, which in its blatant nationalism comes precariously close to comparing the Lord to one who controls or manages a prostitute, is that Tyre will become a subject of Israel and her God. Tyre’s commercial profits will be used to enrich the Lord’s people.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and it will be like the people, like the priest.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like the servant, like his master.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like the female servant, like her mistress.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like the buyer, like the seller.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like the lender, like the borrower.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “like the creditor, just as the one to whom he lends.”
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “for the Lord has spoken this word.”

*Translator's note:* Some prefer to read “land” here, but the word pair אֶרֶץ/תֵּבֵל (ʾerets/tevel [see the corresponding term in the parallel line]) elsewhere clearly designates the earth/world (see {{1 Samuel 2:8|1 Sam 2:8}}; 1 Chr 16:30; {{Job 37|Job 37}}; {{Job 12|12}}; {{Psalm 19:4|Pss 19:4}}; {{Psalm 24:1|24:1}}; {{Psalm 33:8|33:8}}; {{Psalm 89:11|89:11}}; {{Psalm 90:2|90:2}}; {{Psalm 96:13|96:13}}; {{Psalm 98:9|98:9}}; {{Proverbs 8:26|Prov 8:26}}, {{Proverbs 8:31|31}}; {{Isaiah 14:16|Isa 14:16-17}}; {{Isaiah 34:1|34:1}}; Jer 10:12; 51:15; Lam 4:12). According to L. Stadelmann, תבל designates “the habitable part of the world” (*The Hebrew Conception of the World* [AnBib], 130).

*Translator's note:* Or “mourns” (BDB 5 s.v. אָבַל). *HALOT* 6-7 lists the homonyms I אבל (“mourn”) and II אבל (“dry up”). They propose the second here on the basis of parallelism.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the height of the people of the earth.” The translation assumes an emendation of the singular form מְרוֹם (merom, “height of”) to the plural construct מְרֹמֵי (merome, “high ones of”; note the plural verb at the beginning of the line), and understands the latter as referring to the prominent people of human society.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “beneath”; cf. KJV, ASV, NRSV “under”; NAB “because of.”

*Study note:* {{Isaiah 26:21|Isa 26:21}} suggests that the earth’s inhabitants defiled the earth by shedding the blood of their fellow human beings. See also {{Numbers 35:33|Num 35:33-34}}, which assumes that bloodshed defiles a land.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “moved past [the?] regulation.”

*Translator's note:* Or “everlasting covenant” (KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT); NAB “the ancient covenant”; CEV “their agreement that was to last forever.”

*Study note:* For a lengthy discussion of the identity of this covenant/treaty, see R. Chisholm, “The ‘Everlasting Covenant’ and the ‘City of Chaos’: Intentional Ambiguity and Irony in {{Isaiah 24|Isaiah 24}}, ” *CTR* 6 (1993): 237-53. In this context, where judgment comes upon both the pagan nations and God’s covenant community, the phrase “permanent treaty” is intentionally ambiguous. For the nations this treaty is the Noahic mandate of {{Genesis 9:1|Gen 9:1-7}} with its specific stipulations and central regulation ({{Genesis 9:7|Gen 9:7}}). By shedding blood, the warlike nations violated this treaty, which promotes population growth and prohibits murder. For Israel, which was also guilty of bloodshed (see {{Isaiah 1:15|Isa 1:15}}, {{Isaiah 1:21|21}}; {{Isaiah 4:4|4:4}}), this “permanent treaty” would refer more specifically to the Mosaic Law and its regulations prohibiting murder ({{Exodus 20:13|Exod 20:13}}; {{Numbers 35:6|Num 35:6-34}}), which are an extension of the Noahic mandate.

*Study note:* Ancient Near Eastern treaties often had “curses,” or threatened judgments, attached to them. (See {{Deuteronomy 28|Deut 28}} for a biblical example of such curses.) The party or parties taking an oath of allegiance acknowledged that disobedience would activate these curses, which typically threatened loss of agricultural fertility as depicted in the following verses.

*Translator's note:* The verb אָשַׁם (ʾasham, “be guilty”) is here used metonymically to mean “pay, suffer for one’s guilt” (see *HALOT* 95 s.v. אשׁם).

*Translator's note:* BDB 359 s.v. חָרַר derives the verb חָרוּ (kharu) from חָרַר (kharar, “burn”), but *HALOT* 351 s.v. II חרה understands a *hapax legomenon* חָרָה (kharah, “to diminish in number,” a homonym of חָרָה) here, relating it to an alleged Arabic cognate meaning “to decrease.” The Qumran scroll 1QIsaa has חורו, perhaps understanding the root as חָוַר (khavar, “grow pale”; see {{Isaiah 29:22|Isa 29:22}} and *HALOT* 299 s.v. I חור).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and mankind is left small [in number].”
*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text reads literally, “all the joyful in heart,” but the context specifies the context as parties and drinking bouts.
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the joy” (again later in this verse).
*Translator's note:* *Heb* “with a song they do not drink wine.”

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the city of chaos” (so NAB, NASB, NRSV). Isaiah uses the term תֹּהוּ (tohu) rather frequently of things (like idols) that are empty and worthless (see BDB 1062 s.v.), so the word might characterize the city as rebellious or morally worthless. However, in this context, which focuses on the effects of divine judgment, it probably refers to the ruined or worthless condition in which the city is left (note the use of the word in {{Isaiah 34:11|Isa 34:11}}). For a discussion of the identity of this city, see R. Chisholm, “The ‘Everlasting Covenant’ and the ‘City of Chaos’: Intentional Ambiguity and Irony in {{Isaiah 24|Isaiah 24}}, ” *CTR* 6 (1993): 237-53. In the context of universal judgment depicted in {{Isaiah 24|Isa 24}}, this city represents all the nations and cities of the world which, like Babylon of old and the powers/cities mentioned in chapters {{Isaiah 13|13-23}}, rebel against God’s authority. Behind the stereotypical language one can detect various specific manifestations of this symbolic and paradigmatic city, including Babylon, Moab, and Jerusalem, all of which are alluded or referred to in chapters {{Isaiah 24|24-27}}.

*Study note:* In the Ugaritic mythological texts Leviathan is a sea creature that symbolizes the destructive water of the sea and in turn the forces of chaos that threaten the established order. Isaiah here applies imagery from Canaanite mythology to Yahweh’s eschatological victory over his enemies. Elsewhere in the OT, the battle with the sea motif is applied to Yahweh’s victories over the forces of chaos at creation and in history (cf. {{Psalm 74:13|Pss 74:13-14}}; {{Psalm 77:16|77:16-20}}; {{Psalm 89:9|89:9-10}}; {{Isaiah 51:9|Isa 51:9-10}}). Yahweh’s subjugation of the chaos waters is related to His kingship (cf. {{Psalm 29:3|Pss 29:3}}, {{Psalm 29:10|10}}; {{Psalm 93:3|93:3-4}}). Apocalyptic literature employs the imagery as well. The beasts of Dan 7 emerge from the sea, while Rev 13 speaks of a seven-headed beast coming from the sea.

*Text-critical note:* The Hebrew text reads literally, “the coming ones, let Jacob take root.” הַבָּאִים (habbaʾim, “the coming ones”) should probably be emended to יָמִים בָּאִים (yamim baʾim, “days [are] coming”) or בְּיָמִים הַבָּאִים (biyamim habbaʾim, “in the coming days”).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “fruit” (so KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).

*Study note:* This apparently refers to a future population explosion. See {{Isaiah 26:18|26:18}}.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text reads literally, “Like the striking down of the one striking him down does he strike him down?” The meaning of the text is unclear, but this may be a rhetorical question, suggesting that Israel has not experienced divine judgment to the same degree as her oppressors. In this case “the one striking…down” refers to Israel’s oppressors, while the pronoun “him” refers to Israel. The subject of the final verb (“does he strike…down”) would then be God, while the pronoun “him” would again refer to Israel.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text reads literally, “Or like the killing of his killed ones is he killed?” If one accepts the interpretation of the parallel line outlined in the previous note, then this line too would contain a rhetorical question suggesting that Israel has not experienced destruction to the same degree as its enemies. In this case “his killed ones” refer to the ones who struck Israel down, and Israel would be the subject of the final verb (“is he killed”).

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text reads literally, “in [?], in sending her away, you oppose her.” The meaning of this line is uncertain. The form בְּסַאסְּאָה (besasseʾah) is taken as an infinitive from סַאסְּאָה (sasseʾah) with a prepositional prefix and a third feminine singular suffix. (The MT does not have a mappiq in the final he [ה], however). According to *HALOT* 738 s.v. סַאסְּאָה the verb is a Palpel form from an otherwise unattested root cognate with an Arabic verb meaning “to gather beasts with a call.” Perhaps it means “to call, summon” here, but this is a very tentative proposal. בְּשַׁלְחָהּ (beshalekhah, “in sending her away”) appears to be a Piel infinitive with a prepositional prefix and a third feminine singular suffix. Since the Piel of שָׁלָח (shalakh) can sometimes mean “divorce” (*HALOT* 1514-15 s.v.) and the following verb רִיב (riv, “oppose”) can be used in legal contexts, it is possible that divorce proceedings are alluded to here. This may explain why Israel is referred to as feminine in this verse, in contrast to the masculine forms used in vv. {{Isaiah 27:6|6-7}} and {{Isaiah 27:9|9}}.

*Translator's note:* The Hebrew text has no object expressed, but one can understand a third feminine singular pronominal object and place a mappiq in the final he (ה) of the form to indicate the suffix.

*Study note:* The “east wind” here symbolizes violent divine judgment.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and this [is] all the fruit of removing his sin.” The meaning of the statement is not entirely clear, though “removing his sin” certainly parallels “Jacob’s sin will be removed” in the preceding line. If original, “all the fruit” may refer to the result of the decision to remove sin, but the phrase may be a textual variation of an original לְכַפֵּר (lekhapper, “to atone for”), which in turn might be a gloss on הָסִר (hasir, “removing”).

Another option is to understand “in this way” and “this” in v. {{Isaiah 27:9|9a}} as referring back to the judgment described in v. {{Isaiah 27:8|8}}. In this case כָּפַר (kafar, “atone for”) is used in a sarcastic sense; Jacob’s sin is “atoned for” and removed through severe judgment. Following this line of interpretation, one might paraphrase the verse as follows: “So in this way (through judgment) Jacob’s sin will be “atoned for,” and this is the way his sin will be removed, when he (i.e., God) makes all the altar stones like crushed limestone….” This interpretation is more consistent with the tone of judgment in vv. {{Isaiah 27:8|8}} and {{Isaiah 27:10|10-11}}.

*Study note:* The identity of this city is uncertain. The context suggests that an Israelite city, perhaps Samaria or Jerusalem, is in view. For discussions of interpretive options see J. N. Oswalt, *Isaiah* (NICOT), 1:496-97, and Paul L. Redditt, “Once Again, the City in {{Isaiah 24|Isaiah 24-27}}, ” *HAR* 10 (1986), 332.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “the river,” a frequent designation in the OT for the Euphrates. For clarity most modern English versions substitute the name “Euphrates” for “the river” here.

*Translator's note:* The meaning of this verse has been debated. The final line says “a little there, a little there,” while the preceding lines have a series of redundancies (כִּי צַו לָצָו צַו לָצָו קַו לָקָו קַו לָקָו, ki tsav latsav, tsav latsav, qav laqav, qav laqav). The present translation assumes that the repetitive syllables are gibberish that resembles baby talk (cf v. {{Isaiah 28:9|9b}}) and mimics what the people will hear when foreign invaders conquer the land (v. {{Isaiah 28:11|11}}). In this case זְעֵיר (zeʿer, “a little”) refers to the short syllabic structure of the babbling (cf. CEV, REB and see *HALOT* 1010 s.v. צַו). Some take צַו (tsav) as a derivative of צָוָה (tsavah, “command”) and translate the first part of the statement as “command after command, command after command.” Proponents of this position (followed by many English versions) also take קַו (qav) as a noun meaning “measuring line” (see v. {{Isaiah 28:17|17}}), understood here in the abstract sense of “standard” or “rule.”

*Study note:* This verse alludes to the coming Assyrian invasion, when the people will hear a foreign language that sounds like gibberish to them. The Lord is the subject of the verb “will speak,” as v. {{Isaiah 28:12|12}} makes clear. He once spoke in meaningful terms, but in the coming judgment he will speak to them, as it were, through the mouth of foreign oppressors. The apparent gibberish they hear will be an outward reminder that God has decreed their defeat.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “who said to them.”

*Study note:* This message encapsulates the Lord’s invitation to his people to find security in his protection and blessing.

In this case the “Lord’s message” is not the foreigner’s strange sounding words (as in v. {{Isaiah 28:10|10}}), but the Lord’s repeated appeals to them (like the one quoted in v. {{Isaiah 28:12|12}}). As time goes on, the Lord’s appeals through the prophets will have no impact on the people; they will regard prophetic preaching as gibberish.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “as a result they will go and stumble backward.” Perhaps an infant falling as it attempts to learn to walk is the background image here (cf. v. {{Isaiah 28:9|9b}}). The Hebrew term לְמַעַן (lemaʿan) could be taken as indicating purpose (“in order that”), rather than simple result. In this case the people’s insensitivity to the message is caused by the Lord as a means of expediting their downfall.

*Study note:* When divine warnings and appeals become gibberish to the spiritually insensitive, they have no guidance and are doomed to destruction.

The parallelism in both verses (note “treaty”) seems to demand a meaning “agreement” for both nouns. Perhaps חֹזֶה and חזוּת are used in a metonymic sense in vv. {{Isaiah 28:15|15}} and {{Isaiah 28:18|18}}. Another option is to propose a homonymic root. See J. N. Oswalt, *Isaiah* (NICOT), 1:514, and *HALOT* 301 s.v. II חֹזֶה.

*Study note:* Verses {{Isaiah 28:23|23-29}} emphasize that God possesses great wisdom and has established a natural order. Evidence of this can be seen in the way farmers utilize divinely imparted wisdom to grow and harvest crops. God’s dealings with his people will exhibit this same kind of wisdom and order. Judgment will be accomplished according to a divinely ordered timetable and, while severe enough, will not be excessive. Judgment must come, just as planting inevitably follows plowing. God will, as it were, thresh his people, but he will not crush them to the point where they will be of no use to him.

*Study note:* The “name” of the Lord sometimes stands by metonymy for the Lord himself, see {{Exodus 23:21|Exod 23:21}}; Lev 24:11; {{Psalm 54:1|Pss 54:1}} (54:3 HT); {{Psalm 124:8|124:8}}. In {{Isaiah 30:27|Isa 30:27}} the point is that he reveals that aspect of his character which his name suggests—he comes as Yahweh (“he is present”), the ever present helper of his people who annihilates their enemies and delivers them. The name “Yahweh” originated in a context where God assured a fearful Moses that he would be with him as he confronted Pharaoh and delivered Israel from slavery in Egypt. See {{Exodus 3|Exod 3}}.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his anger burns, and heaviness of elevation.” The meaning of the phrase “heaviness of elevation” is unclear, for מַשָּׂאָה (massaʾah, “elevation”) occurs only here. Some understand the term as referring to a cloud (elevated above the earth’s surface), in which case one might translate, “and in heavy clouds” (cf. NAB “with lowering clouds”). Others relate the noun to מָשָׂא (masaʾ, “burden”) and interpret it as a reference to judgment. In this case one might translate, “and with severe judgment.” The present translation assumes that the noun refers to his glory and that “heaviness” emphasizes its degree.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his lips are full of anger, and his tongue is like consuming fire.” The Lord’s lips and tongue are used metonymically for his word (or perhaps his battle cry; see v. {{Isaiah 30:31|31}}).

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “his breath is like a flooding river.” This might picture the Lord breathing heavily as he runs down his enemy, but in light of the preceding verse, which mentions his lips and tongue, “breath” probably stands metonymically for the word or battle cry that he expels from his mouth as he shouts. In {{Isaiah 34:16|Isa 34:16}} and {{Psalm 33:6|Ps 33:6}} the Lord’s “breath” is associated with his command.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “shaking nations in a sieve of worthlessness.” It is not certain exactly how שָׁוְא (shaveʾ, “emptiness, worthlessness”) modifies “sieve.” A sieve is used to separate grain from chaff and isolate what is worthless so that it might be discarded. Perhaps the nations are likened to such chaff; God’s judgment will sift them out for destruction.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “and a bit that leads astray [is] in the jaws of the peoples.” Here the nations are likened to a horse that can be controlled by a bit placed in its mouth. In this case the Lord uses his sovereign control over the “horse” to lead it to its demise.

*Translator's note:* *Heb* “[you will have] joy of heart, like the one going with a flute to enter the mountain of the Lord to the Rock of Israel.” The image here is not a foundational rock, but a rocky cliff where people could hide for protection (for example, the fortress of Masada).
